title: Scalar Variables - Text & String Concatenation
description: Variables are how robots store information. Store text values and combine them to create messages—no more hardcoding repeated text everywhere.

story.setup: The ship's systems are coming online, but you notice something in the diagnostic logs.
story.context: We're typing the ship name and status codes repeatedly. What if we need to change them? We'd have to update dozens of places. There's a better way—store values in variables and reuse them.
story.success: Excellent! You've stored text in variables and combined them into messages. This is fundamental—variables let us write flexible, maintainable code!

instructions: Create a test named 'Ship Status Report'
Store the ship name in a variable '${ship_name}' with value 'SYNTAX-IV'
Store the status in a variable '${status}' with value 'operational'
Combine the variables to create a status message and log it: 'Ship SYNTAX-IV status: operational'
Inspect the Console tab to see how variables were combined
hints: Variables can be concatenated by placing them next to text in Log
You can also use Set Variable to concatenate first, then log

theory.title: Scalar Variables & Primitive Data Types
theory.content:
The ship's diagnostic panel flickers. You notice the same ship name appearing twelve times in the logs.

See that? We're typing 'SYNTAX-IV Explorer' everywhere. If we need to rename the ship, we'd have to update it in dozens of places. That's inefficient and error-prone. We need variables.

What Are Scalar Variables?

A scalar variable stores a single value—text, a number, or a boolean. Think of it like a labeled storage container.

Creating Scalar Variables

You can create scalar variables in different ways:

# Method 1: Set Variable keyword
${name}    Set Variable    PROTO-7

# Method 2: Assignment with = (just visual style, works the same)
${name}=    PROTO-7

# Method 3: Return value from any keyword
${result}    15

All three work identically. The = is just decoration—Robot Framework ignores it. Choose what looks clearest to you.

What Can Variables Store? Strings!

In Robot Framework, text is called a string. When you store something in a variable, it becomes a string:

${ship}    Set Variable    SYNTAX-IV
${code}    Set Variable    42
${status}    Set Variable    true

All three are strings. Even 42 is stored as text "42", not a number. Robot Framework treats everything as text unless a keyword explicitly converts it. This makes variables simple—you don't have to worry about types most of the time.

Variable Names Are Flexible

Here's something surprising about Robot Framework—variable names are really forgiving:

# These are ALL the same variable:
${myVar}
${MyVar}
${MYVAR}
${my_var}
${my var}
${m_y_v_a_r}

Robot Framework normalizes names by:

  • Ignoring case: ${name} = ${NAME}
  • Treating spaces and underscores the same: ${my_var} = ${my var}
  • Ignoring extra spaces/underscores: ${my__var} = ${my_var}

So ${ShipName}, ${ship_name}, and ${SHIP NAME} are the same variable. This is by design—Robot Framework wants to be readable, not picky about formatting.

Combining Text: Concatenation

You'll often need to combine variables with text. That's called concatenation—just a fancy word for "put text together." Here's how:

# Method 1: Embed variables directly in text
${name}    Set Variable    PROTO-7
${status}    Set Variable    active
Log    Robot ${name} is ${status}
# Output: Robot PROTO-7 is active

# Method 2: Build a message variable first
${name}    Set Variable    PROTO-7
${status}    Set Variable    active
${message}    Set Variable    Robot ${name} is ${status}
Log    ${message}
# Output: Robot PROTO-7 is active

# Method 3: Use Catenate keyword (adds spaces for you)
${message}    Catenate    Robot    ${name}    is    ${status}
# Output: Robot PROTO-7 is active

The first method is most common—just put ${variable} wherever you want the value inserted.

Why Bother With Variables?

You might wonder—why not just type the text directly? Here's why variables matter:

  • Change once, fix everywhere: Update the ship name in one place, not fifty
  • Reuse values: Define "testuser@example.com" once, use it ten times
  • Readable code: ${ship_status} is clearer than a mysterious "operational"
  • Easy updates: Swap test data without touching test logic

Real-World Example

*** Test Cases ***
Login Test
    ${username}    Set Variable    testuser@example.com
    ${password}    Set Variable    SecurePass123
    
    Log    Attempting login with ${username}
    Input Text    id=username    ${username}
    Input Text    id=password    ${password}
    Click Button    id=login
    
    # If username changes, update it once above
